author: Supreme Court of New Jersey (Poritz, C.J.)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses the relationship between professional-conduct rules, civil liability and discovery sanctions, not AI capability, selective deployment, verification or legal-work redesign. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to assess the cluster’s principal proposition.

st.t: Lawyer accountability: Discipline and liability remain separate
st.an: Baxt directly supports the cluster’s central distinction: professional-conduct rules govern discipline and do not independently create civil liability, but relevant rules may inform duty and the standard of care within an otherwise recognised civil claim. It also distinguishes discipline’s public-protection purpose from compensation for individual harm.
qs: clear that the purpose of the Model Rules was to regulate lawyer conduct through the disciplinary process, not to serve as a basis for civil liability.”               FN2.

kp.k: Professional rules do not independently create civil liability
kp.d: The Supreme Court of New Jersey rejected a new cause of action against an adversary's attorneys based solely on violations of the New Jersey Rules of Professional Conduct. The opinion concerns professional accountability rather than AI. It distinguished disciplinary regulation from independently actionable civil wrongs, drawing support from existing New Jersey decisions and the ABA Model Rules' Scope section. The court expressly noted that New Jersey had not adopted that explanatory material.
qs: We decline to do so today.
They are not designed**275           to be a basis for civil liability.

kp.k: Ethical rules can inform independently established tort claims
kp.d: The court distinguished creating a cause of action from using pertinent professional rules to assess duties and standards of care in existing claims. Its discussion of Albright, Tedards and Petrillo covered fiduciary duty, negligence, abuse of process and negligent misrepresentation. Citing Allen, the court qualified this evidentiary use: the rule must protect someone in the plaintiff's position or address the particular harm suffered.
qs: the court was required to determine whether, in the factual context, a duty was owed by an attorney to third parties.

kp.k: Discipline protects public and professional integrity
kp.d: The court explained that disciplinary proceedings serve purposes different from private civil litigation. Quoting the Washington Supreme Court's Hizey opinion, it emphasized that discipline can apply without damage or an otherwise actionable civil wrong. It also reasoned that aspirational professional standards, including courtesy and consideration, can be inappropriate predicates for civil actions. It rejected the plaintiffs' argument that an independent RPC-based action was necessary to ensure compliance.
qs: The rationale is the need for protection of the public and the integrity of the profession.
that individual is not a party to the proceeding.

kp.k: Concealment requires more than misleading document provenance
kp.d: Although the tortious-concealment claim was not preserved for Supreme Court review, the court offered substantive observations explaining why these facts did not establish it. Drawing on Viviano, it identified a disclosure obligation, material information, inability readily to obtain that information independently, intentional nondisclosure and harm through reliance. Here, counsel could identify the agreement's source from her own client's files; provenance did not resolve enforceability, and the agreement was relatively insignificant in the foreclosure dispute. The court distinguished concealment of provenance from destruction or substantial alteration of evidence.
qs: We conclude that a claim based on tortious concealment has not been preserved for review by this Court.FN5
These facts do not make out a claim for tortious concealment of evidence.

kp.k: Discovery misconduct remains sanctionable without an independent tort
kp.d: The court condemned the attorneys' deliberate obstruction during at least one month in November–December 1991: they placed a signed agreement obtained from Grove's files into the bank's files and withheld candid answers about its source. It identified reasonable expenses under Rules 4:23-3 and 4:23-4 as an available remedy. In the case's unique settlement circumstances, plaintiffs could move within 30 days under Rule 4:50-1(f) to reopen the foreclosure dismissal solely to seek those expenses. The trial court would determine misconduct and any fee award; the Supreme Court did not itself award damages or fees.
qs: Such conduct appears on its face to violate the New Jersey Rules Governing Civil Practice and the Rules of Professional Conduct.
The relief sought here-attorney's fees and costs-would have been available under those rules.FN7
defendants cannot raise the privilege as a defense in a discovery sanctions proceeding.

kp.k: Ethics reporting operates alongside discovery sanctions
kp.d: The court invoked New Jersey RPC 8.3(a), requiring reporting when known misconduct raises a substantial question about another lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness. It stated that Grove's attorney should have reported the alleged violations when they occurred and referred the defendants' conduct to the Office of Attorney Ethics. It instructed plaintiffs to notify that office whether they would pursue discovery sanctions so that disciplinary review could be stayed until the civil action ended.
qs: shall inform the appropriate professional authority.
Plaintiffs should inform the OAE whether they intend to pursue sanctions against defendants for discovery violations in order that the OAE may stay its review until the civil action is completed.
